# Introduction {#sec-intro}

## Background and Problem Statement {#sec-background}

Market research helps businesses understand what customers want. But it is expensive. A professional study usually costs between \$8,000 and \$15,000 [@lin2026]. Most small businesses in the San Gabriel Valley (SGV) cannot pay that. So they make big decisions, like pricing, new products, or where to open, based on guesses.

:::::: stat-strip
::: stat
[\$8K–15K]{.num} [cost of one professional study]{.lbl}
:::

::: stat
[4]{.num} [SGV industries we study]{.lbl}
:::

::: stat
[\~600]{.num} [real people used as a benchmark]{.lbl}
:::
::::::

AI may offer a cheaper option. Recent studies show that large language models (LLMs) can act like survey respondents. When given a profile, such as age, income, and location, an LLM can answer survey questions in ways that often look like real people's answers [@argyle2023; @aher2023; @horton2023]. In marketing, researchers have used this to estimate what customers are willing to pay and how they see competing brands [@brand2023; @li2024; @wang2026].

There is a catch. AI answers are not always right. They can be too confident, too uniform, or biased toward certain groups [@bisbee2024]. A common finding is that AI tends to get the order right (which option people prefer most) but gets the exact numbers wrong (how much they prefer it). Dr. Lin describes this as "trust the order, test the level" [@lin2026]. This means AI research is only useful if it is checked against real data first.

Our client is the Tarkington Business Futures Institute (TBFI), a new applied "Do Tank" inside Cal Poly Pomona's College of Business Administration [@cpp2026; @tbfi2026]. TBFI wants to offer low-cost research to local businesses. It faces three problems:

:::::: card-grid
::: card
[👥]{.icon}<br>**Training doesn't scale**

Training new consultants one by one takes too long.
:::

::: card
[🖥️]{.icon}<br>**No live demo**

Businesses want to see a working demo, not a slide deck.
:::

::: card
[💰]{.icon}<br>**Research costs too much**

Local businesses need research they can afford and trust.
:::
::::::

## Project Objectives (POs) {#sec-po}

The project has four main goals [@lin2026]:

::::::: card-grid
::: card
[🎮]{.icon}<br>**PO1. Build the Do Tank Simulator**

A browser-based training game that walks a user through a full consulting job: intake, research design, AI survey panel, perceptual map, and client readout. At least 10 rounds, plus a short version TBFI can use as a sales demo.
:::

::: card
[📊]{.icon}<br>**PO2. Build the SGV Insights Dashboard**

AI-generated customer insights for four industries: specialty food and beverage, ADU and prefab housing, cross-border e-commerce and logistics, and health and senior services. Includes perceptual maps, customer segments, and a trust report.
:::

::: card
[📣]{.icon}<br>**PO3. Run a digital marketing plan**

A landing page, LinkedIn and email content, and outreach to local chambers of commerce. We track the full funnel, from site visits to client meetings.
:::

::: card
[🎓]{.icon}<br>**PO4. Train the first consultant group**

New consultants go through the simulator, and we measure their skills before and after.
:::
:::::::

### AO1. Evidence Review and Data Setup (Simran Kaur ) {#sec-ao1}

::: ao-panel
[Question: What does current research say, and what data do we have?]{.q}
:::

This AO gathers what we already know. It reviews published studies on AI survey respondents and collects public data for each industry, such as Census ACS, County Business Patterns, and Esri Tapestry. The output is a short summary of the evidence and a clean data set that the other AOs can build on.

### AO2. Perceptual Maps and Customer Segments (Simran Kaur) {#sec-ao2}

::: ao-panel
[Question: How do customers see brands in each industry, and what groups do they fall into?]{.q}
:::

This AO turns the AI survey data into pictures that business owners can read at a glance. For each of the four industries, it will build two things.

**Perceptual maps** place competing brands on a simple chart based on how customers see them, for example cheap versus premium, or traditional versus modern. Brands that sit close together are seen as similar, and empty spaces on the map can point to gaps in the market. We will follow the approach of @li2024, who showed that LLMs can produce perceptual maps that closely match those built from real customer surveys.

**Customer segments** group respondents who want similar things, such as price-focused shoppers or quality-first buyers. Each segment gets a short profile describing who they are, what they care about, and how to reach them.

Because AI tends to get rankings right more often than exact numbers, the maps will focus on where brands sit relative to each other, not on precise scores [@lin2026]. Only results that pass the AO3 validation checks will go on the dashboard. The output is a set of maps and segment profiles for each industry, built into the SGV Insights Dashboard (PO2).

### AO3. Validating the AI Panels (Gabriela Raygoza Quintero) {#sec-ao3}

::: ao-panel
[Question: Can we trust the AI panels? How closely do they match real people?]{.q}
:::

This AO focuses on whether the AI respondents can be trusted as a reliable source. We will provide the same survey to three LLM (ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini) and compare their responses to the pre-existing human benchmark of approximatley 600 participants. [@lin2026].

In order to determine the validity of the LLM's, the Structured Taxonomy AI Measurement Protocool (STAMP) will be implemented in order to to construct the necessary measurement. We will use two main scores. **Krippendorff's alpha** checks whether different panels agree with each other, with values of 0.80 or above treated as strong and 0.67 as the minimum [@krippendorff2018]. **F1 score** checks how often the AI's answers match the human answers. Following *"trust the order, test the level,"* we will first check whether the AI ranks options in the same order as people, and then check how far off its exact numbers are.

The result will sort each finding into one of three groups: **use as is**, **use for rankings only**, or **do not use**. This tells TBFI and its clients how much to trust each result on the dashboard.

### AO4. Simulator Build and Training Results (Yushan Huang) {#sec-ao4}

::: ao-panel
[Question: Does the simulator improve consultant skills?]{.q}
:::

This AO develops the simulator's rounds and evaluates whether it works as a training tool for new consultants. The simulator will provide a structured environment where consultants can practice interpreting research results, making decisions, and applying insights to realistic consulting scenarios.

To evaluate the training results, new consultants will complete a skills check before and after using the simulator. Their pre-training and post-training scores will be compared to measure changes in performance. The results will help determine whether the simulator improves the skills it is designed to teach and identify areas where the training experience may need further improvement.

### AO5. Marketing Funnel Analytics (Veronica Vega) {#sec-ao5}

::: ao-panel
[Question: Which marketing channels bring in real client inquiries?]{.q}
:::

The Assessment Objective (AO) for this project will measure the success of the digital marketing plan by tracking the performance of potential clients through the entire marketing funnel. The digital marketing funnel includes: website visits representing awareness and interest in the company and services provided through the website; demo completions, intake inquiries and meetings with sponsors.

**A comparison** of the baseline data from before the campaign was launched and the resulting data after the campaign has been implemented will show the impact of the marketing and measure the effectiveness of the campaign. The assessment also aims to establish which of the various marketing channels such as SEO (search engine optimization), social media, email marketing, referral networks and paid online advertising. Which have generated the highest volume of qualified intake inquiries leading to sponsor acquisitions. The results will be used for data driven decision making and to optimize future online marketing investments to maximize return.

**Previous research** suggests that interactive marketing channels are often more effective at generating customer inquiries and conversions than traditional channels. Specifically, search engine optimization (SEO), online review platforms, and word-of-mouth referrals were found to increase customer acquisition rates for service organizations [@majid2021]. These findings support the need to evaluate which marketing channels generate the greatest number of qualified intake inquiries and sponsor meetings for TBFI.

## Significance of the Project {#sec-significance}

This project matters to three groups.

:::::: card-grid
::: card
[🏪]{.icon}<br>**Local businesses**

Get research they could not afford before. A bakery or a senior care provider in the SGV can learn what customers want without spending \$10,000.
:::

::: card
[🏛️]{.icon}<br>**TBFI**

Gets working tools, a sales demo, and its first clients. The simulator lets TBFI train new consultants faster, so the program can grow.
:::

::: card
[🔬]{.icon}<br>**The research field**

Gets a real-world test of AI survey panels. Most studies so far were run in labs [@argyle2023; @bisbee2024]. We test the method on actual local businesses.
:::
::::::

For our team, the project builds skills that employers want: working with AI tools, testing data quality, building dashboards, and running digital campaigns.
